newsitem.title: USA: Fla. cop cleared, then suspended in riot shooting.
newsitem.headline: Fla. cop cleared, then suspended in riot shooting.

text.p: A Florida grand jury ruled on Wednesday that a white police officer was justified in shooting and killing a young black motorist whose death sparked a night of rioting.
"We have determined the death of Tyron Lewis was the result of a justifiable homicide under Florida law," Pinellas County State Attorney Bernie McCabe said after the 16-member grand jury acted.
The decision prompted fears of more violence in St. Petersburg, where police stepped up patrols in the riot area and community leaders appealed for calm.

Following the grand jury ruling, the police department suspended Officer James Knight, who shot Lewis, for 60 days without pay for violating its firearms policy. Knight's attorney, Joseph Ciarciaglino, said he would appeal.

But the grand jury ruled the death of Lewis was justifiable homicide because Knight was in danger of being run over by the car Lewis was driving after he and his partner, Sandra Minor, pulled Lewis over for speeding.

Knight, 34, appeared before the grand jury on Tuesday to provide his account. He has been on administrative leave since the shooting. Minor, one of the first witnesses to testify in the case, returned on Tuesday to testify a second time.

The fatal shooting of Lewis, 18, during what seemed a routine traffic stop on Oct. 24 was followed by hours of rioting in south St. Petersburg, a predominantly black section of this western Florida city.
At least 11 people were hurt, mostly police officers, and nearly 30 fires were set in shops, businesses and homes before police regained control early the next morning.

Black youths in the city charged they were constantly victimised by police. Community leaders said poverty, lack of jobs and bleak prospects for blacks in St. Petersburg created resentment that fuelled the unrest. The incident also prompted federal investigations.
Officials pledged an enhanced police presence in the riot area Wednesday night, where community reaction was mixed.
Truman Smith, who raised Lewis, said of the ruling: "To kill my son and then to clear the officer is unthinkable."
Erica Serrmons, a black worker at a barbecue shop across the road from the scene of the shooting, said the ruling could have been unfair because the grand jury had only one black.

"Most people here, young people especially, feel the decision was not good enough," Serrmons said. "But I suppose that he was investigated and if the process was fair then it should be accepted by the public."
